title: Pods
summary: What a Pod is, init and sidecar containers, lifecycle phases, restart policy, health probes and static Pods.

blocks.text: On a cargo ship, containers aren't loaded one by one. They go into a **bay**: a reserved slot with its own phone number (the Pod IP), a shared power line, and a shared locker (volumes). Containers in the same bay talk over the bay intercom (`localhost`). The port tracks bays, not loose containers, and a bay always sits on one ship (node).

A Pod is the **smallest deployable unit** in Kubernetes: one or more containers that share network and storage, plus a spec saying how to run them. Its containers are always placed on the same node and scheduled together.

items: **One container per Pod** is the most common pattern; Kubernetes manages the Pod, not the container.
Put several containers in one Pod only when they are tightly coupled. Don't do it for replication: run more Pods instead.
Each Pod gets its own IP address. Its containers share the network namespace, so they reach each other on `localhost` and must not clash on ports.
Volumes declared in the Pod are visible to every container in it.
You rarely create bare Pods. Use a workload resource such as a Deployment, Job or StatefulSet, whose controller replaces failed Pods.
A Pod is an environment, not a process. Restarting a container is not the same as restarting the Pod.

blocks.text: Most of a running Pod is immutable. Updates may only change `spec.containers[*].image`, `spec.initContainers[*].image`, `spec.activeDeadlineSeconds`, `spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, `spec.tolerations` (add only) and `spec.schedulingGates`.

Before any cargo goes into a bay, a **prep crew** goes in first: one worker sweeps, the next checks the power, the next confirms the customer has paid. They go one at a time, in order, and each must finish before the next starts. Only then is the real cargo loaded. If the bay has to be set up again, the whole prep crew repeats its checklist.
Init containers live in the `initContainers` field and run **before** the app containers. Use them for setup tools or to wait for a dependency.

items: They always run to completion, **one at a time, in order**. Each must succeed before the next starts.
On failure the kubelet keeps restarting the init container. If the Pod's `restartPolicy` is `Never`, the whole Pod is marked failed instead.
Regular init containers don't support `lifecycle`, `livenessProbe`, `readinessProbe` or `startupProbe`.
While they run the Pod stays `Pending`, its `Initialized` condition is false and `kubectl get` shows a status like `Init:0/2`.
If the Pod restarts, every init container runs again, so make their code idempotent.
Check one with `kubectl logs <pod> -c <init-container>`.

blocks.text:
spec:
  initContainers:
  - name: <init-name>
    image: busybox:1.28
    command: ['sh', '-c', '<wait-or-setup-command>']
  containers:
  - name: <app-name>
    image: <image>

Some cargo needs company for the whole voyage, such as a **cooling unit** clipped to a container of fish, or a GPS tracker. That helper boards early, stays running alongside the cargo the entire trip, and is switched off only after the cargo is unloaded. That is a sidecar.
A native sidecar is an entry in `initContainers` with `restartPolicy: Always`. Instead of exiting, it keeps running for the Pod's whole life, alongside the app (stable since v1.33).

items: It starts in init order. The next init container waits until the sidecar has started (or its `startupProbe` passes).
It supports probes. A sidecar's `readinessProbe` feeds into whether the Pod is ready.
It can be restarted on its own without touching the main container.
At shutdown, sidecars stop **after** the main containers, in reverse order of declaration.
A sidecar does not stop a Job from completing once the main container finishes.
Typical uses: logging, monitoring, security or data sync.

blocks.text:
initContainers:
- name: logshipper
  image: alpine:latest
  restartPolicy: Always
  command: ['sh', '-c', 'tail -F /opt/logs.txt']

Every bay has a status on the harbor office board. **Pending**: booked, waiting for a ship or for cargo to arrive. **Running**: at sea. **Succeeded**: delivered. **Failed**: something went wrong for good. **Unknown**: the ship has gone quiet on the radio. A bay never moves to another ship. If its ship sinks, the office books a brand-new bay somewhere else.

rows: Accepted, but containers not ready to run yet (includes scheduling and image pulls)
Bound to a node, all containers created, at least one running, starting or restarting
All containers exited successfully and won't restart
All containers terminated, at least one in failure
The Pod's state couldn't be obtained, usually a node communication problem

items: Each container is **Waiting**, **Running** or **Terminated**. `kubectl describe pod <name-of-pod>` shows them, with a reason or exit code.
`CrashLoopBackOff` and `Terminating` are kubectl display statuses, not phases.
A Pod is scheduled once. It is never moved to another node; a controller creates a new Pod with a new UID instead.
Graceful termination defaults to **30 seconds** (`terminationGracePeriodSeconds`). The kubelet sends TERM, then KILL when time runs out.

blocks.text: For a Pod stuck in `CrashLoopBackOff`, start with `kubectl logs <name-of-pod>` for the app error, then `kubectl describe pod <name-of-pod>` for events such as failed probes or config problems.

When a container's machinery stops mid-voyage, the ship's **cargo officer** (the kubelet) follows the bay's standing rule: always restart it, restart only if it broke, or never touch it. If it keeps breaking, the officer waits a little longer before each retry so they don't spend the whole trip fixing one box.
The Pod-level `restartPolicy` covers app containers and regular init containers. It takes `Always` (the default), `OnFailure` or `Never`.

items: Deployments allow only `Always`. Jobs usually use `OnFailure` or `Never`.
Sidecars ignore the Pod policy because their own container-level `restartPolicy` is `Always`.
Restarts use exponential back-off: 10s, 20s, 40s and so on, capped at 300 seconds (5 minutes).
After a container runs cleanly for 10 minutes, the back-off timer resets.
Restart policy only covers replacement containers inside the same Pod, on the same node.

blocks.text: Inspectors walk the deck with three questions. **Startup**: "Has this slow unit finished warming up?" (the other inspectors wait until it has). **Liveness**: "Is it still working?" If not, it is restarted. **Readiness**: "Can it take deliveries right now?" If not, it is taken off the delivery list for a while, but left alone.

rows: kubelet kills the container; restartPolicy applies
Container marked not ready; Pod removed from Service endpoints. Runs for the whole lifecycle
kubelet kills the container. Liveness and readiness wait until it succeeds

items: Each probe uses exactly one mechanism: `exec` (exit code 0), `httpGet` (status 200 to 399), `tcpSocket` (port open) or `grpc` (response SERVING).
Defaults: `initialDelaySeconds` 0, `periodSeconds` 10, `timeoutSeconds` 1, `successThreshold` 1, `failureThreshold` 3.
`successThreshold` must be 1 for liveness and startup probes.
Liveness doesn't wait for readiness. Delay it with `initialDelaySeconds` or a startup probe.
A container with no probe of a given kind counts as Success for it.

blocks.text:
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 10
  periodSeconds: 5
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /ready
    port: 8080
A badly designed liveness probe can cause cascading failures by restarting containers under load. It should only fail when the app truly can't recover, such as a deadlock.

Most cargo is booked through the harbor office. But a ship's officer can also load cargo straight from a **logbook in their own cabin** (a manifest directory on the node). The office shows only a **mirror** entry for it. Crossing out the mirror entry at the office does nothing; you have to go aboard and change the logbook.
A static Pod is defined by a manifest file on one node and run directly by that node's kubelet. Set `staticPodPath: <the directory>` in the kubelet config, e.g. `/etc/kubernetes/manifests`.

items: The kubelet rescans the directory and creates or removes Pods as files appear or disappear.
The API server shows a **mirror Pod**, named in the example as `static-web-my-node1` (Pod name plus node). Labels are copied to it.
`kubectl delete pod` on the mirror Pod doesn't stop the static Pod.
Files starting with a dot are skipped, but extensions are not filtered. A `.backup` copy in that directory also gets run.
On the node, inspect with `crictl ps` and `crictl logs <container_id>`.
The `--pod-manifest-path` kubelet flag is the deprecated alternative; `--manifest-url` / `staticPodURL` loads a manifest from a URL.

blocks.text: To remove or change a static Pod, SSH to its node and move or edit the file in the manifest directory (e.g. `mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/<file>.yaml /tmp`). Keep backups outside that directory.

flashcards.back: The smallest deployable unit: one or more containers sharing network and storage, scheduled together on one node.

flashcards.front: How do containers in the same Pod talk to each other?
flashcards.back: Over `localhost`. They share the Pod's IP and port space.
No. It's a kubectl status meaning restarts are in back-off.
10s, 20s, 40s and so on, capped at 300s (5 min); resets after 10 min of clean running.
Sequentially, in order, each to completion, before any app container starts.

questions.stem: Two containers in the same Pod need to talk over the network. What address should one use to reach the other?

options.text: localhost, on the other container's port
options.explanation: Containers in a Pod share the network namespace.

options.text: The other container's own IP address
options.explanation: Containers in a Pod don't get separate IPs; they share the Pod's.
Services are for reaching Pods, not containers in the same Pod.

options.text: They can't communicate over the network
options.explanation: They can, via localhost.

questions.stem: Which fields of a running Pod can be changed with an ordinary update? Select 2.

options.explanation: One of the few mutable fields.
Mutable, within limits.
Namespace, name and uid are immutable.
Resources change through the resize subresource, not a regular update.

questions.stem: A Pod's containers have all exited, and one exited with a non-zero code. The Pod has restartPolicy: Never. What phase is it in?

options.explanation: All containers terminated and at least one failed.
Succeeded needs every container to exit successfully.
Pending is before containers are set up.
That is a kubectl status, not a phase, and Never means no restarts.

questions.stem: A container exits with code 0. Under which restartPolicy is it restarted?

options.explanation: Always restarts after any termination.
OnFailure restarts only on non-zero exit.
Never doesn't restart at all.
Always does restart it.

questions.stem: The delay between container restarts keeps doubling with no upper limit.

options.explanation: The back-off is capped at 300 seconds (5 minutes).
Correct. It starts at 10s, doubles, and caps at 300s.

questions.stem: A Pod shows STATUS CrashLoopBackOff. What is the most direct first step to find the cause?

options.explanation: The lifecycle docs call checking logs the most direct way to diagnose.
The issue is inside the container, not the node.

options.text: Change the Pod's restartPolicy to Always
options.explanation: Restarts are what's already happening.
Switches clusters; it doesn't diagnose.

questions.stem: A Pod has two init containers. The first never completes. What does kubectl get pods show?

options.text: A status like Init:0/2, and the app container hasn't started
options.explanation: Init containers run in order and block app containers.

options.text: Running, with both init containers running in parallel
options.explanation: Init containers run one at a time.
Nothing has completed.

options.text: The app container starts once the second init container finishes
options.explanation: The second can't start until the first succeeds.

questions.stem: Which statements about regular init containers are true? Select 3.

options.text: They run sequentially and each must succeed before the next
options.explanation: Stated directly in the docs.
Validation rejects it.

options.text: They all run again if the Pod restarts
options.explanation: So their code should be idempotent.

options.text: They keep running alongside the app containers
options.explanation: That describes sidecars; init containers run to completion.

questions.stem: You want a log shipper that starts before the app and keeps running for the Pod's lifetime. How do you declare it as a native sidecar?

options.explanation: That's how Kubernetes defines a sidecar.
Containers there are app containers, and Never stops restarts.
That is a regular init container that must exit.

options.text: As a second entry under containers
options.explanation: That works as a plain multi-container Pod, but gives no start ordering and isn't a native sidecar.

questions.stem: In a Job, a native sidecar container stops the Job from completing because it never exits.

options.explanation: Native sidecars don't block Job completion once the main container finishes.
Correct. The Job can complete while its sidecar was still running.

questions.stem: A container's readiness probe starts failing while its liveness probe still passes. What happens?

options.text: The Pod is removed from matching Services' endpoints but the container keeps running
options.explanation: Readiness failure means no traffic, not a restart.
That's what a liveness or startup failure does.

options.text: The Pod is rescheduled to another node
options.explanation: Pods are never moved between nodes.

options.text: Nothing; readiness only matters at startup
options.explanation: Readiness probes run during the whole lifecycle.

questions.stem: Which probe defaults are correct? Select 3.

options.explanation: Probes run every 10 seconds by default.
Default timeout is 1 second.
Three failures in a row by default.
It defaults to 0. 30 seconds is the default Pod termination grace period.

questions.stem: A slow app needs up to 5 minutes to start, but you want liveness to react quickly afterwards. What does the probes task page recommend?

options.text: Add a startupProbe on the same endpoint with failureThreshold: 30 and periodSeconds: 10
options.explanation: 30 x 10 = 300s to start; then liveness takes over.

options.text: Set the liveness probe's failureThreshold to 1
options.explanation: That makes liveness react even faster; it gives no extra startup time. The page pairs it with a startup probe.

options.text: Replace the liveness probe with a readiness probe
options.explanation: Readiness doesn't restart deadlocked containers.
That disables restarts entirely.

questions.stem: You run kubectl delete pod on a static Pod's mirror Pod. What happens?

options.text: The static Pod keeps running and still appears in kubectl get pods
options.explanation: Deleting the mirror Pod doesn't make the kubelet remove the static Pod.

options.text: The static Pod stops for good
options.explanation: Only removing the manifest file stops it.

options.text: The kubelet deletes the manifest file
options.explanation: The Pod is removed only when you move the file out of the directory yourself.
The delete succeeds, but the Pod is still running afterwards.

questions.stem: Before editing a static Pod manifest you ran cp kube-apiserver.yaml kube-apiserver.yaml.backup in the manifest directory. What's the risk?

options.text: The kubelet also reads the backup, so the outdated spec may take effect
options.explanation: Extensions aren't filtered; only dot-files are skipped.

options.text: None; the kubelet only reads files ending in .yaml
options.explanation: There is no filtering by extension.
It tries to create a Pod from each file.

options.text: The API server deletes the backup
options.explanation: The API server doesn't touch node files.

questions.stem: Start a single `nginx` Pod named `nginx` in the namespace `mynamespace`.
questions.explanation: `kubectl run` creates one Pod; `-n` (`--namespace`) chooses where.
